post_text:
We spent three weeks debating whether to sync our legacy billing migration with a distributed event stream or a dual-write proxy.

I pushed for the proxy, wrapping both systems in a dull Java interface backed by a nightly SQL reconciliation script.

Slack was quiet.

The team wanted Kafka and CDC, arguing that my approach looked dated and added latency to the write path.

I spent evenings second-guessing the decision, terrified that my hesitation around complex streaming infrastructure was holding our platform back.

Seven months later, an unhandled timezone edge case in the legacy database silently dropped transactions during daylight saving time.

Because our boring reconciliation job simply diffed raw rows on a cron, it caught the drift instantly, allowing us to repair the state before finance noticed.

There were no late-night heroics or frantic war rooms. We patched the missing records quietly, verified parity across both schemas, and decommissioned the legacy engine two weeks later without ceremony.

What I learned:

Conservative architecture trades cleverness upfront for the simple visibility needed to survive unexpected failures.
